title: Appendix D — Computer Networks Supplement
text:
D.1 Introduction
Section 6.1 gives a web application programmer what they need to know about computer networks to understand the following chapter and those that follow it: that communication is organised into layers, that these layers have names and responsibilities, and that concepts such as IP, port, MAC or DNS are not loose abstractions, but concrete pieces of that system. This appendix goes deeper into this subject beyond what is strictly necessary to develop web applications, much as a painter does not need to know how to make their own paint to paint a picture, but benefits from understanding how it is made. Here, for whoever wants that deeper dive, is the complete formalism of services and protocols, the exact, field-by-field structure of TCP, IP and Ethernet headers, and the complete encapsulation process in the OSI model.

title: Appendix D — Computer Networks Supplement
section: D.2 The Real Protocols per Layer
text:
D.2 The Real Protocols per Layer
Section 6.2 presents the two reference models, OSI and TCP/IP, and the three TCP/IP layers most relevant to a web programmer. The following figure brings the two models together, showing how the OSI layers group into the four TCP/IP layers, and some of the concrete protocols that run in each: HTTP, used by Contraponto, shares the application layer with SMTP (email), FTP (file transfer) or DNS, a subject explored further in Section 6.6; the transport layer is dominated by TCP and UDP; and the network layer by IP.






Figure D.1: The two models side by side, with the most common protocols in each layer.

title: Appendix D — Computer Networks Supplement
text:
D.3 Services and Protocols
Two concepts are central to understanding, in detail, how layers communicate with one another: services and protocols.
A service represents a set of functions offered to a user by a provider. That service is made available through Service Access Points (SAPs): from the perspective of whoever uses the service, all of its characteristics are fully defined by the interface at the SAP, which means the entity providing the service can be treated as completely abstract, with no need to know how that service is implemented internally. It is exactly this principle that allows a web application programmer to use TCP without needing to understand how it guarantees, internally, the reliable delivery of data.






Figure D.2: On the left, the user of a service exchanges messages with the provider of that service through a SAP, without knowing its internal implementation; on the right, the same principle applied to the OSI and TCP/IP layers.



A protocol, in turn, is a family of standards for exchanging information: a set of rules that define the physical connections, the data formats, the transmission models, and the means used to ensure correctness against errors and failures in data transmission. While the service describes what a layer offers to the layer above it, the protocol describes how two entities of the same layer, one on the client side and the other on the server side, communicate with each other to implement that service.

title: Appendix D — Computer Networks Supplement
section: D.4 The Structure of the Headers

title: Appendix D — Computer Networks Supplement
text:
D.5 Data Reception, in Detail
Section 6.3 describes, in summary, the reception process: each layer removes the header that the corresponding layer had added to it on the sending side, until only the application’s original data remains. In detail, layer by layer: the physical layer detects a signal with the Ethernet address matching the local network interface, and passes the information to the link layer; this checks whether the destination MAC address is its own and, if so, passes the information to the network layer; this checks whether the destination IP address is its own and, if so, passes the information to the transport layer; and this, finally, checks whether there is an application registered on the indicated destination port and, if so, finally delivers the data to it.






Figure D.6: The reverse path to sending: the signal arrives through the network card and climbs the layers, one by one, up to the application.

title: Appendix D — Computer Networks Supplement
text:
D.6 An Overall View
The same encapsulation and decapsulation principle applies, in even finer detail, to the complete OSI model, with its seven layers: in each one, on the sending side, a new header is added (AH at the application layer, PH at the presentation layer, SH at the session layer, and so on); on the receiving side, each layer removes the header that corresponds to it, in a process entirely similar to what was already seen for TCP/IP, just with more layers involved:






Figure D.7: The complete encapsulation and decapsulation process in the OSI model, from sender to receiver.



It is worth reviewing, in summary, which address is added by each layer along this path: the transport layer adds the source and destination ports, the network layer the source and destination IP addresses, and the link layer the source and destination MAC addresses, each one wrapping around the data already prepared by the previous layer:






Figure D.8: The different types of address added at each layer: port (transport), IP (network) and MAC (link).

title: Appendix E — HTTP Supplement
text:
E.1 Introduction
Section 7.2 gives a web application programmer what they need to know about the HTTP protocol to understand the rest of this book: what the GET and POST methods are, how a request reaches a virtual resource, how PHP receives that data through the superglobals, and how a site keeps track of a reader’s state through cookies and sessions, despite HTTP being, by nature, stateless. This appendix goes deeper into this subject beyond what is strictly necessary to develop web applications, much as a painter does not need to know how to make their own paint to paint a picture, but benefits from understanding how it is made. Here, for whoever wants that deeper dive, is the exact syntax of GET and POST messages, other common headers, the strategies browsers use to manage connections, and the complete set of cookie attributes.

title: Appendix E — HTTP Supplement
section: E.2 The Exact Syntax of HTTP Messages

title: Appendix E — HTTP Supplement
text:
E.3 HTTP Headers
Section 7.6 presents the Host header, the only mandatory one in a request. Another common header is Accept, which tells the server what content types (MIME formats) the browser prefers to receive in the response, in order of preference, indicated by a quality value q between 0 and 1 (the default value is 1, maximum preference):
GET /artigos.php?categoria=Cultura HTTP/1.1
Host: contraponto.pt
Accept: text/html, application/xhtml+xml, application/xml;q=0.9, */*;q=0.8
In this example, the browser prefers HTML, accepts XML with a slightly lower preference, and accepts any other content type (*/*) only as a last resort.

title: Appendix E — HTTP Supplement
Appendix E — HTTP Supplement
section: E.5 The Attributes of a Cookie
text:
E.5 The Attributes of a Cookie
Section 7.9.1 presents the essentials about cookies: a small piece of information the server asks the browser to store and resend with each following request. Cookies are defined, in detail, in the RFC 6265 standard, HTTP State Management Mechanism.
A server can set several cookies at the same time, each with its own meaning, for example a session identifier and the reader’s preferred language:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: sessao=31d4d96e407aad42; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly
Set-Cookie: lang=pt-PT; Path=/; Domain=contraponto.pt
A cookie set by the server can include several attributes, besides the name-value pair:

Expires or Max-Age: define when the cookie should expire (a concrete date, or a number of seconds, respectively); if both are set, Max-Age takes precedence. With neither of the two, the cookie expires when the browser is closed;
Domain and Path: restrict which host and which folder on the server the cookie is sent to;
Secure: the browser only sends this cookie over a secure channel, HTTPS;
HttpOnly: an important protection against XSS attacks, a subject explored further in Section 9.1; the cookie is only exchanged between browser and server, without being accessible to client-side JavaScript code.

To delete a cookie, the server resends it with an expiry date already in the past; from that point on, the browser stops including it in following requests. Note also that cookies are limited to 4kB of information each. In PHP, a cookie is created with the setcookie() function, which accepts all of these attributes as parameters:
<?php
setcookie(
    "utilizador",   // nome
    "joao",         // valor
    time() + 3600,  // expira em 1 hora
    "/",            // path
    "",             // domain
    true,           // secure
    true            // httponly
);
